title: Wanting the clarinet, Chicago trombone players, and band discipline
summary: Jackson never got the clarinet, lists good Chicago trombonists, credits a marching band for his discipline, and mentions Oliver's household and red beans and rice.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Well I wanted to play the clarinet.

Did you ever get the clarinet at all? That's why it'd take me so long with the trombone, see. No, never did, nothing but the trombone. After I began to play it and people would take notes and I'd say well I'd just go ahead on through with it. I'm glad I did now. Because they told me, he says, there isn't but a few, at that time you didn't have the musicians they have now, everywhere you look, he says there ain't but a few good trombone players around here. And I held the top up top there around here, not bragging, for years around here. And just like Roy told me, he says, you learn that trombone if you learn it right, he says, you'll hold your line. And at one time there was Blake, Al Wynn, myself, and this boy would die. Billy, he was a singer too, he died. There was about four of us, and Taylor, there was about four or five. Blake was a good one, Al was good, and this boy Taylor was good, he played with O. Hines when he was at the old Grand Territory. He's dead now too. Yeah. And it came in and the advice he gave to me when I sat down in the pit and played them overtures and things. Well now, here's another man, I must attribute my success, what success I had, Art Stewart, the big K.P. band, morning, noon, and night and things like that. He always hollering at me, get in there! All right, I go to New York with a brass band, about eighty pieces. I don't know how to walk and step. I attribute that to them fellas hollering at me, get in the step there, rookie, get in the step there. We went to New York in the 20s there, but it must have been a hundred and some pieces, Bob Shaffin, the best cream of Chicago. And we walked from Harlem to Central Park. We taught New York Open. We played a concert in a little town out of New York. We camped right on Boston Road out there. Oh I could just talk for years but I just jumped from one place to another. Now Joe had a nice wife and a daughter named Ruby. I visited Joe's house so many times I just can't count. I ate that gumbo and whatnot. He had a cruel wife. Somebody said he was a big eater, is that right? Oh my goodness, red beans and rice. Now that's Louis Armstrong when they had the band Savoy. They had them parties and red beans and rice. They go to some lady's house there on South Park and she's cooking the red beans and rice, and that's when they had Clarence Black's band and Louis's band, later on they had it. Now that's a man, Charlie Elder.
